text: Figure 4 shows a task-specific compromise between episode reward and training time, not a monotonic learning benefit from more robots. The simplified task reduces maximum stair and obstacle heights and removes the curriculum so improving policies are not assigned harder terrain. Rewards are reported as means and standard deviations over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, increasing robot count shortens each robot's rollout and training time, but reward drops sharply at excessive counts. The authors link this decline to insufficient temporal information for generalized advantage estimation; throughput gains also slow beyond roughly 4,000 robots. With fewer robots, reward decreases gradually, which the authors suggest reflects less diverse, correlated samples. Larger batches improve reward and postpone the decline but take longer to train. The 20,000-robot, million-sample baseline yields the highest reported reward at greater training cost, not under a matched batch budget. About 2,048-4,096 robots with roughly 100,000-200,000 samples per batch offer the reported balance for this task, reflecting temporal-data requirements and slowing throughput gains.

Terrain-aware locomotion training requires fast simulation without sacrificing temporal experience. We keep Isaac Gym simulation and proximal policy optimization (PPO) on one GPU, reducing data transfers while collecting experience from thousands of robots. An adaptive curriculum promotes or demotes each robot according to traversal performance by relocating it among tiled terrain levels, changing difficulty without regenerating the shared mesh. The policy uses proprioception and local terrain heights; training incorporates friction randomization, observation noise, pushes, and actuator modeling for transfer. PPO uses large minibatches and time-out bootstrapping, but increasing robot count at fixed batch size shortens rollouts and can impair learning. On an i9-11900k workstation with an NVIDIA RTX A6000, ANYmal C training with 4,096 robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 updates took under 20 minutes. Simulated crossings without base contact achieved nearly 100% success for stair steps up to 0.2 m; obstacle success declined with difficulty, and slope climbing failed beyond 25 degrees. The fixed policy traversed stairs and obstacles on physical ANYmal C, but imperfect lidar-derived terrain maps reduced robustness, prompting a 0.6 m/s linear-velocity command limit. These experiments support rapid training and deployment under the tested temporal, terrain, and sensing conditions.

Proximal policy optimization (PPO) uses a critic to estimate an infinite-horizon discounted return, so failure or goal completion and time-limit resets require different treatment. Failures and completed goals can be anticipated from the state; a time-out cannot, because observations omit episode time. Treating a time-out as terminal would therefore remove continuation value for a reason the critic cannot observe, truncating its target rather than reflecting task completion. The environment flags time-outs separately and augments their rewards with the critic's own discounted prediction of future return, bootstrapping the interrupted trajectory's target instead of assigning zero continuation value. This prediction concerns the trajectory cut short, not the episode started after reset. Episodes last up to 20 seconds and span multiple short rollout batches because environments are not reset after each policy update. Time-outs can consequently occur inside a batch and must be handled wherever they occur, not merely at collection boundaries.

Rapid terrain-aware locomotion training must accelerate data collection without sacrificing the experience needed for learning. We keep Isaac Gym simulation, observation and reward computation, and proximal policy optimization on one GPU to reduce CPU-GPU transfers. An adaptive curriculum relocates robots among prebuilt terrain tiles according to traversal progress, raising difficulty after success and lowering it after insufficient progress. This combines parallel collection with progressively challenging experience without regenerating terrain. A single policy follows motion commands using proprioception and local terrain heights. With 4,096 robots, 98,304 samples per batch, and 1,500 policy updates, an ANYmal C policy trains in under 20 minutes on an i9-11900k/RTX A6000 workstation. However, increasing robot count at fixed batch size shortens individual rollouts, and inadequate consecutive steps can undermine learning. Simulation traversal without base contact is nearly always successful on stairs up to 0.2 m, but success declines on randomized obstacles and climbing fails beyond 25-degree slopes. The fixed policy also traverses stairs and obstacles on hardware, where imperfect elevation maps reduce robustness and prompt a maximum linear-velocity command of 0.6 m/s. The reported configuration therefore supports rapid training and physical deployment, constrained by rollout duration and terrain sensing.

Figure 4 shows that faster data collection improves the reward-time trade-off only while per-robot trajectories remain long enough for learning. The comparison removes the curriculum, reduces maximum stair and obstacle difficulty, and reports mean episode reward and standard deviation over five runs after 1,500 policy updates. At fixed batch size, more robots mean fewer consecutive steps per robot: training becomes faster, but reward drops sharply at excessive parallelism. The authors explain this drop through insufficient temporal information for advantage estimation; they tentatively attribute the smaller reward decline at low robot counts to reduced sample diversity. Throughput scales nearly linearly to about 4,000 robots before gains slow. Larger batches increase reward and permit more robots before deterioration, at greater training cost. The million-sample, 20,000-robot baseline attains the highest reward but takes longer to train. Thus, about 2,048-4,096 robots with roughly 100,000-200,000 samples per batch offer the reported compromise on this simplified task, balancing trajectory length, diversity, and throughput rather than licensing unlimited parallelism.

In proximal policy optimization (PPO), the critic estimates an infinite-horizon discounted return. A failure or goal completion is a task termination the critic can anticipate. A time limit, however, interrupts a continuing task without an observable warning: episode time is absent from the observations. Treating this reset like a failure would remove the continuation value from the target, even though the task did not end for a predictable reason. The modified environment interface therefore identifies time-outs separately. For these transitions, the reward is augmented with the critic's discounted estimate of remaining return, bootstrapping its target rather than assigning zero future return. This handling cannot assume that time-outs occur only at batch boundaries: episodes last up to 20 seconds and span multiple short rollout batches. Completing a collection batch does not reset the environment; time-limit resets must be detected wherever they occur.
